full_judgment: In the above case the accused were charged of abetting some known persons who were charged with murder but subsequently the said accused were charged with abetting some unknown persons and hence they were acquitted on the ground of defect of charge. In the present case, none of course has been charged with the commission of the principal offence of murder of deceased Maziron Nassa, but even then the appellant has been charged with the abetment of the murder and therefore, the learned Advocate for the appellant submits that the charge of abetment levelled against the accused appellant cannot be sustained. The point raised in the instant case cannot be decided relying on the decision quoted above as the facts and circumstances of the two cases and the point at issue are different and distinguishable. Besides the applicability of the principle laid down in the cited decision let us see whether the abetment has been proved against the accused appellant. In the present case, there is absolutely no evidence which could constitute the offence of abetment of murder against a person known or unknown. The prosecution evidence is insufficient and inadequate to inspire any confidence so as to hold that the deceased Maziron Nessa was murdered in the house of the accused and the evidence is absolutely nil as to how, when and whom the accused appellant abetted the offence of murder. In the abetment of murder, the learned trial court seems to have been guided by sentiment only relying on facts that the death took place in the house of the appellant and the defence failed to substantiate its plea that it was the case of suicide. It is true that death took place in the house of the accused appellant but the prosecution witnesses themselves said that the accused appellant was away from the house at the time of occurrence as they went to the hat and returned after the occurrence after sunset. It is also true, that the defence plea that it was a case of suicide has remained unsubstantiated, but failure on the part of the defence to prove defence plea, even if taken, does not react on the defence case because it is always the burden of the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and this burden never shifts on the defence so as to falsify the prosecution case and also to prove innocence of the accused appellant. Prosecution must stand on its own legs. From the mere fact that the death occurred in the house of accused-appellant, there could be no adverse presumption against the accused appellant and the prosecution must discharge its burden in proving the case of murder and the abetment thereof, amount of proof must be very strict and conclusive and evidence must be of unimpeachable character which is lacking in the present case.
